claim: TANGO1 binds and exports Procollagen VII from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
source: TANGO1 binds and exports Procollagen VII from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known finding that sets up the study.

claim: The cytoplasmic domain of TANGO1 connects to SLY1.
source: In this study, we report a connection between the cytoplasmic domain of TANGO1 and SLY1, a protein that is required for membrane fusion.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Knockdown of SLY1 by siRNA arrested Procollagen VII in the ER.
source: Knockdown of SLY1 by siRNA arrested Procollagen VII in the ER without affecting the recruitment of COPII components, general protein secretion, and retrograde transport of the KDEL-containing protein BIP, and ERGIC53.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by western blot and microscopy data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: SLY1 knockdown does not affect the recruitment of COPII components.
source: Knockdown of SLY1 by siRNA arrested Procollagen VII in the ER without affecting the recruitment of COPII components, general protein secretion, and retrograde transport of the KDEL-containing protein BIP, and ERGIC53.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4 showing unchanged levels of COPII components and Figure 8 showing SEC31 localization.

claim: SLY1 knockdown does not affect general protein secretion.
source: Knockdown of SLY1 by siRNA arrested Procollagen VII in the ER without affecting the recruitment of COPII components, general protein secretion, and retrograde transport of the KDEL-containing protein BIP, and ERGIC53.
evidence: This is supported by metabolic labeling data in Figure 6A showing no effect on bulk protein secretion.

claim: SLY1 knockdown does not affect retrograde transport of the KDEL-containing protein BIP and ERGIC53.
source: Knockdown of SLY1 by siRNA arrested Procollagen VII in the ER without affecting the recruitment of COPII components, general protein secretion, and retrograde transport of the KDEL-containing protein BIP, and ERGIC53.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5 showing normal localization of BIP and ERGIC53 cycling.

claim: SLY1 interacts with the ER-specific SNARE proteins Syntaxin 17 and 18.
source: SLY1 is known to interact with the ER-specific SNARE proteins Syntaxin 17 and 18, however only Syntaxin 18 was required for Procollagen VII export.
evidence: This is stated as known information from the literature.

claim: Only Syntaxin 18 was required for Procollagen VII export.
source: SLY1 is known to interact with the ER-specific SNARE proteins Syntaxin 17 and 18, however only Syntaxin 18 was required for Procollagen VII export.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 9 showing that STX18 but not STX17 knockdown blocks PC VII secretion.

claim: Neither SLY1 nor Syntaxin 18 was required for the export of Procollagen I from the ER.
source: Neither SLY1 nor Syntaxin 18 was required for the export of the equally bulky Procollagen I from the ER.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figures 6C, 6E, and 9F showing normal PC I secretion upon SLY1 or STX18 knockdown.

claim: There exist different export pathways for secretory cargoes from the ER.
source: Altogether, these findings reveal the sorting of bulky collagen family members by TANGO1 at the ER and highlight the existence of different export pathways for secretory cargoes one of which is mediated by the specific SNARE complex containing SLY1 and Syntaxin 18.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential requirements for SLY1/STX18 in PC VII vs PC I export.

claim: One export pathway is mediated by the specific SNARE complex containing SLY1 and Syntaxin 18.
source: Altogether, these findings reveal the sorting of bulky collagen family members by TANGO1 at the ER and highlight the existence of different export pathways for secretory cargoes one of which is mediated by the specific SNARE complex containing SLY1 and Syntaxin 18.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the requirement of both SLY1 and STX18 for PC VII export.

claim: Collagens are the most abundant secretory proteins, comprising 25–30% of the human body dry weight.
source: Collagens are the most abundant secretory proteins, comprising 25–30% of the human body dry weight (Pataridis et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pataridis et al., 2008.

claim: Collagens are required for cell attachment, tissue organization and remodeling, and for the differentiation of chondrocytes to produce mineralized bones.
source: They are required for cell attachment, tissue organization and remodeling, and for the differentiation of chondrocytes to produce mineralized bones (Gelse et al., 2003; Wilson et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gelse et al., 2003 and Wilson et al., 2011.

claim: There are at least 28 different kinds of collagens.
source: There are at least 28 different kinds of collagens, composed of homo or hetero trimers of polypeptide chains coiled around each other to form a triple helix (Shoulders and Raines, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shoulders and Raines, 2009.

claim: Collagens are composed of homo or hetero trimers of polypeptide chains coiled around each other to form a triple helix.
source: There are at least 28 different kinds of collagens, composed of homo or hetero trimers of polypeptide chains coiled around each other to form a triple helix (Shoulders and Raines, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shoulders and Raines, 2009.

claim: Collagen triple helices can be up to 450 nm long, as in the case of Collagen VII.
source: These unbendable triple helices, which can be up to 450 nm long, as in the case of Collagen VII, are too big to fit into the conventional transport carriers of the secretory pathway that have been identified thus far (Malhotra and Erlmann, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Malhotra and Erlmann, 2011.

claim: Collagen triple helices are too big to fit into the conventional transport carriers of the secretory pathway.
source: These unbendable triple helices, which can be up to 450 nm long, as in the case of Collagen VII, are too big to fit into the conventional transport carriers of the secretory pathway that have been identified thus far (Malhotra and Erlmann, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Malhotra and Erlmann, 2011.

claim: TANGO1 has been identified for its requirement in the export of Procollagen VII from the ER in tissue culture cells.
source: A protein called TANGO1 has been identified for its requirement in the export of Procollagen VII (PC VII) from the ER in tissue culture cells (Saito et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Saito et al., 2009.

claim: The knockout of TANGO1 in mice results in the production of a pup that dies at birth due to defective bone mineralization.
source: The knockout of TANGO1 in mice results in the production of a pup that dies at birth due to defective bone mineralization.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wilson et al., 2011.

claim: The cause of death in TANGO1 knockout mice is a block in the secretion of multiple collagens needed for the differentiation of chondrocytes.
source: The cause is a block in the secretion of multiple collagens needed for the differentiation of chondrocytes (Wilson et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wilson et al., 2011.

claim: TANGO1 is required for collagen secretion in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: TANGO1 is also required for collagen secretion in Drosophila melanogaster (Pastor-Pareja and Xu, 2011; Lerner et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pastor-Pareja and Xu, 2011 and Lerner et al., 2013.

claim: TANGO1 binds PC VII via its SH3 domain in the lumen of the ER.
source: TANGO1 binds PC VII via its SH3 domain in the lumen of the ER (Saito et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Saito et al., 2009.

claim: TANGO1 binds cTAGE5 on the cytoplasmic side.
source: On the cytoplasmic side, TANGO1 binds cTAGE5 and both these proteins contain a proline rich domain that interacts with the COPII components SEC23/24 (Saito et al., 2009, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Saito et al., 2009 and 2011.

claim: Both TANGO1 and cTAGE5 contain a proline rich domain that interacts with the COPII components SEC23/24.
source: On the cytoplasmic side, TANGO1 binds cTAGE5 and both these proteins contain a proline rich domain that interacts with the COPII components SEC23/24 (Saito et al., 2009, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Saito et al., 2009 and 2011.

claim: Binding of PC VII to TANGO1 in the lumen promotes the binding of TANGO1's proline rich domain to SEC23/24.
source: We have proposed that binding of PC VII to TANGO1 in the lumen promotes the binding of TANGO1's proline rich domain to SEC23/24.
evidence: This is a proposed model from the authors' previous work.

claim: TANGO1 binding to SEC23/24 retards the recruitment of SEC13/31 to SEC23/24 and thus delays the events leading to the biogenesis of the COPII vesicle.
source: This retards the recruitment of SEC13/31 to SEC23/24 and thus delays the events leading to the biogenesis of the COPII vesicle (Malhotra and Erlmann, 2011).
evidence: This is a proposed model supported by a citation to Malhotra and Erlmann, 2011.

claim: Upon growth to a size that is large enough to encapsulate PC VII, TANGO1 dissociates from both PC VII and SEC23/24.
source: Upon growth to a size that is large enough to encapsulate PC VII, TANGO1 dissociates from both PC VII and SEC23/24.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model for PC VII export.

claim: The binding of SEC13/31 to SEC23/24 completes the assembly of COPII components on a patch of the ER.
source: The binding of SEC13/31 to SEC23/24 completes the assembly of COPII components on a patch of the ER.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on known COPII assembly mechanisms.

claim: PC VII is exported presumably in a mega carrier from the ER.
source: These events then lead to the export of PC VII, presumably in a mega carrier from the ER (Saito et al., 2009, 2011).
evidence: This is a proposed model supported by citations to Saito et al., 2009 and 2011.

claim: Ubiquitination of SEC31 by the CUL3-KLHL12 ligase complex has been reported to control the exit of Procollagen I from the ER.
source: Ubiquitination of SEC31 by the CUL3-KLHL12 ligase complex has been reported to control the exit of Procollagen I (PC I) from the ER (Jin et al., 2012; Malhotra, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jin et al., 2012 and Malhotra, 2012.

claim: Sedlin is reported to help in the export of PC I and II from the ER by regulating the cycling of SAR1 activation state.
source: Sedlin is reported to help in the export of PC I and II from the ER by regulating the cycling of SAR1 activation state that is essential for COPII assembly at the ER (Venditti et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Venditti et al., 2012.

claim: TANGO1 is not required for PC I export from the ER.
source: TANGO1 is not required for PC I export from the ER, and it is not known whether PC II export is TANGO1 dependent.
evidence: This is stated as known information and is supported by data in Figure 6C and 6E.

claim: It is not known whether PC II export is TANGO1 dependent.
source: TANGO1 is not required for PC I export from the ER, and it is not known whether PC II export is TANGO1 dependent.
evidence: This is stated as an unknown in the field.

claim: COPII components are required for the export of procollagens from the ER.
source: Together these data indicate that COPII components are required for the export of procollagens from the ER, however, they also suggest the possibility that not all procollagens exit the ER by the same mechanism.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the literature and the current study.

claim: Not all procollagens exit the ER by the same mechanism.
source: Together these data indicate that COPII components are required for the export of procollagens from the ER, however, they also suggest the possibility that not all procollagens exit the ER by the same mechanism.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential requirements for TANGO1, SLY1, and STX18 in PC VII vs PC I export.

claim: SLY1 is a member of the STXBP/unc-18/SEC1 family of proteins that regulate the assembly or the activity of SNAREs in membrane fusion events.
source: SLY1 is a member of the STXBP/unc-18/SEC1 family of proteins that regulate the assembly or the activity of SNAREs in membrane fusion events (Carr and Rizo, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Carr and Rizo, 2010.

claim: The yeast ortholog SLY1 is an essential gene.
source: The yeast ortholog SLY1, an essential gene, has been described as a single copy suppressor of the YPT1 deletion (Dascher et al., 1991) and implicated in forward and retrograde trafficking (Ossig et al., 1991; Li et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dascher et al., 1991, Ossig et al., 1991, and Li et al., 2005.

claim: Yeast SLY1 has been described as a single copy suppressor of the YPT1 deletion.
source: The yeast ortholog SLY1, an essential gene, has been described as a single copy suppressor of the YPT1 deletion (Dascher et al., 1991) and implicated in forward and retrograde trafficking (Ossig et al., 1991; Li et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dascher et al., 1991.

claim: Yeast SLY1 is implicated in forward and retrograde trafficking.
source: The yeast ortholog SLY1, an essential gene, has been described as a single copy suppressor of the YPT1 deletion (Dascher et al., 1991) and implicated in forward and retrograde trafficking (Ossig et al., 1991; Li et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ossig et al., 1991 and Li et al., 2005.

claim: A temperature sensitive mutant of Sly1 in zebra fish is not lethal on the cellular level but rather creates developmental defects in embryonic stages.
source: In contrast with its essential roles in yeast, a temperature sensitive mutant of Sly1 in zebra fish is not lethal on the cellular level but rather creates developmental defects in embryonic stages (Nechiporuk et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nechiporuk et al., 2003.

claim: In mammals, SLY1 has been reported to function in conjunction with Syntaxin 5 in the ER to Golgi transport.
source: In mammals, SLY1 has been reported to function in conjunction with Syntaxin 5 (STX5) in the ER to Golgi transport and might also function in the assembly of pre-Golgi intermediates (Rowe et al., 1998) together with Syntaxin 18 (STX18) (Yamaguchi et al., 2002) and Syntaxin 17 (STX17) (Steegmaier et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rowe et al., 1998.

claim: SLY1 might function in the assembly of pre-Golgi intermediates together with Syntaxin 18 and Syntaxin 17.
source: In mammals, SLY1 has been reported to function in conjunction with Syntaxin 5 (STX5) in the ER to Golgi transport and might also function in the assembly of pre-Golgi intermediates (Rowe et al., 1998) together with Syntaxin 18 (STX18) (Yamaguchi et al., 2002) and Syntaxin 17 (STX17) (Steegmaier et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rowe et al., 1998, Yamaguchi et al., 2002, and Steegmaier et al., 2000.

claim: SLY1 has been shown to interact with the COG4 complex and suggested to play a role in intra Golgi and retrograde transport.
source: SLY1 has been shown to interact with the COG4 complex and suggested to play a role in intra Golgi and retrograde transport (Laufman et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Laufman et al., 2009.

claim: In mammalian cells, the proposed roles of SLY1 in traffic between ER and Golgi membranes are based entirely on the use of artificial temperature sensitive mutant protein VSVG and the artificial cargo ss-GFP.
source: It is important to note that in mammalian cells, these proposed roles of SLY1 in traffic between ER and Golgi membranes are based entirely on the use of artificial temperature sensitive mutant protein Vesicular Stomatitis Virus (VSV)-Glycoprotein (G) protein and the artificial cargo signal sequence (ss)-Green Fluorescent Protein (GFP).
evidence: This is a critical assessment of the existing literature.

claim: The role of SLY1 in the trafficking of endogenous cargoes and its potential mechanism of action is a matter of debate.
source: The role of SLY1 in the trafficking of endogenous cargoes and its potential mechanism of action is therefore a matter of debate.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: SLY1 was identified in a mass spectrometry screen for proteins that cross-link to the cytoplasmic domain of TANGO1.
source: To search for proteins that interact with cytoplasmically oriented portions of TANGO1, we expressed a Myc-His tagged version of a truncated form of TANGO1 (TANGO1ct) that lacks the luminal domain in HeLa cells. After crosslinking with membrane permeable DSP and lysis, proteins were recovered on a Nickel agarose column and analyzed by mass spectrometry. Of interest was the finding of SLY1 in the pool of proteins cross-linked to TANGO1.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding described in the Results section.

claim: SLY1 is present in the TANGO1 immunoprecipitate.
source: Our data show the presence of SLY1 in the TANGO1 immunoprecipitate (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: A pool of SLY1-GFP colocalizes with the ER exit sites specific COPII component SEC31 after prepermeabilization.
source: After prepermeabilization of the cells with saponin and extensive washes to remove the cytoplasmic pool of proteins before fixation, a pool of SLY1-GFP was found to colocalize with the ER exit sites specific COPII component SEC31 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A perinuclear SLY1-containing and SEC31-lacking pool partially overlaps with GM130, a marker of the early Golgi cisternae.
source: In addition, a perinuclear SLY1-containing and SEC31-lacking pool was observed. This perinuclear pool of SLY1 partially overlaps with GM130, a marker of the early Golgi cisternae (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Most of SLY1 is Golgi localized, but a small pool co-localizes with Sec31.
source: Our data show that although most of SLY1 was Golgi localized, we detected a small pool that co-localized with Sec31.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the immunofluorescence data in Figure 1B.

claim: It is not known whether recruitment of SLY1 to the ER exit site is by direct binding to TANGO1 or indirectly through other proteins on the cytoplasmic side.
source: At present, we do not know whether recruitment of SLY1 to the ER exit site is by direct binding to TANGO1 or indirectly through other proteins on the cytoplasmic side.
evidence: This is stated as an unknown mechanism.

claim: SLY1 knockdown reduced PC VII secretion by approximately 75% compared with control cells.
source: Quantitation of the ratio of the secreted to intracellular PC VII revealed a 75% reduction upon SLY1 knockdown compared with control cells.
evidence: This is supported by western blot quantitation data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: PC VII secretion was 90% reduced upon TANGO1 knockdown, compared with control cells.
source: PC VII secretion was 90% reduced upon TANGO1 knockdown, compared with control cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot quantitation data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In SLY1 knockdown cells, PC VII accumulated in large structures that also contained the collagen-specific protein chaperone Hsp47.
source: In SLY1 knockdown cells, on the other hand, PC VII accumulated in large structures that also contained the collagen-specific protein chaperone Hsp47 (Saga et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2D and 2E.

claim: Large patches of PC VII are evident in RDEB/FB/C7 cells depleted of TANGO1.
source: Similar large patches of PC VII are also evident in RDEB/FB/C7 cells depleted of TANGO1, which is well known for its role in the export of PC VII from the ER (Saito et al., 2009, 2011) (Figure 2D, upper panel).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2D and citations to Saito et al., 2009 and 2011.

claim: PC VII does not accumulate in the Golgi membranes upon knockdown of either SLY1 or TANGO1.
source: We did not observe accumulation of PC VII in the Golgi membranes upon knockdown of either SLY1 or TANGO1 (Figure 2D, lower panel).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: SLY1 knockdown arrests PC VII in the ER where it accumulates in large patches.
source: Based on these data, we suggest that SLY1 knockdown arrests PC VII in the ER where it accumulates in large patches.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the immunofluorescence and western blot data.

claim: In control cells, gold-conjugated secondary antibodies used to visualize anti-Collagen VII antibody were found distributed throughout the ER.
source: In control cells, gold-conjugated secondary antibodies used to visualize anti-Collagen VII antibody were found distributed throughout the ER.
evidence: This is supported by immunoelectron microscopy data shown in Figure 3.

claim: In SLY1 knockdown cells, PC VII was observed in large patches within dilated ER.
source: In SLY1 knockdown cells, however, PC VII was observed in large patches within dilated ER (Figure 3) but smaller vesicles that could correspond to intermediates en route were not visible.
evidence: This is supported by immunoelectron microscopy data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Smaller vesicles that could correspond to intermediates en route were not visible in SLY1 knockdown cells.
source: In SLY1 knockdown cells, however, PC VII was observed in large patches within dilated ER (Figure 3) but smaller vesicles that could correspond to intermediates en route were not visible.
evidence: This is an observation from immunoelectron microscopy data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Similar patches of PC VII were evident upon knockdown of TANGO1.
source: Similar patches of PC VII were also evident upon knockdown of TANGO1 (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunoelectron microscopy data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The level of SAR1 did not change upon SLY1 or TANGO1 knockdown.
source: The level of SAR1, the initiator of the COPII vesicle budding process, did not change upon SLY1 or TANGO1 knockdown.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The levels of SEC23A and SEC31 were unchanged upon SLY1 or TANGO1 knockdown.
source: Also unchanged were the levels of the other COPII components that are required for the export of secretory cargo, including components of the extracellular matrix, from the ER, specifically SEC23A (Boyadjiev et al., 2006) and SEC31 (Jin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4 and citations to Boyadjiev et al., 2006 and Jin et al., 2012.

claim: The levels of β-COP and ε-COP were unchanged upon SLY1 or TANGO1 knockdown.
source: Because of the possible involvement of SLY1 in the retrograde trafficking pathway, we also tested components of the COPI coat: β-COP and ε-COP, and their levels were also unchanged (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4.

claim: GRP78/BIP was localized to the ER in SLY1 knockdown cells and control cells.
source: GRP78/BIP was localized to the ER in SLY1 knockdown cells and control cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: GRP78/BIP was not detected in the medium collected from control, SLY1- or TANGO1-depleted cells.
source: Moreover, GRP78/BIP was not detected in the medium collected from control, SLY1- or TANGO1-depleted cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Knockdown of TANGO1 or SLY1 did not affect the kinetics of ERGIC53 redistribution to the ER.
source: Knockdown of TANGO1 or SLY1 did not affect the kinetics of ERGIC53 redistribution to the ER (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by the rapamycin-induced trapping assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Under the experimental conditions, knockdown of SLY1 or TANGO1 does not affect retrograde trafficking.
source: We therefore conclude that under our experimental conditions, knockdown of SLY1 or TANGO1 does not affect retrograde trafficking.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figure 5.

claim: Retention of PC VII in the ER, upon knockdown of SLY1 or TANGO1, is not because of a defect in cycling of a component that is specifically required for the constitutive trafficking between the ER and the early Golgi cisternae.
source: Retention of PC VII in the ER, upon knockdown of SLY1 or TANGO1, is therefore not because of a defect in cycling of a component that is specifically required for the constitutive trafficking between the ER and the early Golgi cisternae.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the retrograde trafficking data.

claim: SLY1 knockdown did not have any appreciable effect on the secretion of newly synthesized proteins as measured by metabolic labeling.
source: Surprisingly, SLY1 knockdown did not have any appreciable effect on the secretion of newly synthesized proteins (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by metabolic labeling data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The overall pattern of polypeptides detected by SDS-PAGE is not affected by SLY1 knockdown.
source: This approach does not reveal the specific polypeptides secreted in a SLY1-dependent manner, but shows that the overall pattern of polypeptides detected by SDS-PAGE is not affected by SLY1 knockdown.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the metabolic labeling data in Figure 6A.

claim: Depletion of SLY1 efficiently blocked secretion of ss-HRP and was comparable to the secretion inhibitory drug BFA.
source: The ratio of secreted to internal HRP shows that depletion of SLY1 efficiently blocked secretion ss-HRP and was comparable to known secretion inhibitory drug BFA.
evidence: This is supported by HRP secretion assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: TANGO1 depletion reduced the secretion of ss-HRP to 50% of that from control cells.
source: TANGO1 depletion reduced the secretion of ss-HRP to 50% of that from control cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by HRP secretion assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The secretion of collagen I is not blocked by knockdown of SLY1 or TANGO1 in RDEB/FB/C7 cells.
source: Our results reveal that the secretion of collagen I is not blocked by knockdown of SLY1 or TANGO1 (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Knockdown of SLY1 or TANGO1 in Saos 2 cells did not affect the secretion of PC I.
source: As in RDEB/FB/C7 cells, knockdown of SLY1 or TANGO1 in Saos 2 cells did not affect the secretion of PC I (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: In both RDEB/FB/C7 and Saos2 cell lines, a marginal increase in the secretion of Collagen I is accompanied by an increase in the internal levels of Collagen I in the knocked down cells.
source: In fact, in both cells lines, we detected a marginal increase in the secretion of Collagen I that is accompanied by an increase in the internal levels of Collagen I in the knocked down cells.
evidence: This is an observation from the western blot data in Figures 6C and 6E.

claim: The increase in Collagen I secretion and internal levels suggests a potential effect on the transcriptional regulation of Collagen I expression rather than a defect in its trafficking.
source: This suggests a potential effect on the transcriptional regulation of Collagen I expression rather than a defect in its trafficking.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Collagen I data.

claim: The assembly of the COPII coat is initiated by the activation of the small GTPase SAR1 by the ER-resident protein SEC12.
source: The assembly of the COPII coat is initiated by the activation of the small GTPase SAR1 by the ER-resident protein SEC12.
evidence: This is established knowledge about COPII assembly.

claim: Active SAR1 recruits the inner coat proteins SEC23/24.
source: Active SAR1 recruits the inner coat proteins SEC23/24.
evidence: This is established knowledge about COPII assembly.

claim: The assembly of the outer coat proteins SEC13/31 completes the biogenesis of COPII vesicles by inactivation of SAR1.
source: The assembly of the outer coat proteins SEC13/31 completes the biogenesis of COPII vesicles by inactivation of SAR1 (Zanetti et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to Zanetti et al., 2012.

claim: TANGO1 links PC VII to the inner COPII coat by interacting with the SEC23/24 complex.
source: TANGO1 links PC VII to the inner COPII coat by interacting with the SEC23/24 complex (Saito et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Saito et al., 2009.

claim: Knockdown of SAR1 A alone had marginal effect on the secretion of PC VII.
source: Knockdown of SAR1 A alone had marginal effect on the secretion of PC VII, whereas the knockdown of SAR1 B was largely ineffective.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The knockdown of SAR1 B was largely ineffective on PC VII secretion.
source: Knockdown of SAR1 A alone had marginal effect on the secretion of PC VII, whereas the knockdown of SAR1 B was largely ineffective.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Knockdown of both SAR1 A and B led to an almost total block in PC VII secretion.
source: However, knockdown of both SAR1 A and B led to an almost total block in PC VII secretion, which accumulated in the cells (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In cells depleted of SAR1 A and B, PC VII accumulated in large structures similar to the patches of PC VII seen in RDEB/FB/C7 cells depleted of TANGO1 or SLY1.
source: In cells depleted of SAR1 A and B, PC VII accumulated in large structures (Figure 7C) similar to the patches of PC VII seen in RDEB/FB/C7 cells depleted of TANGO1 or SLY1 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: In cells depleted of SAR1 A and B, SEC31 localized mostly in the cytosol and almost no SEC31 positive punctae were visible.
source: Here, SEC31 localized mostly in the cytosol and almost no SEC31 positive punctae were visible (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: In control cells, PC VII accumulated in the ER in large patches similar to that observed in SLY1 or TANGO1 knockdown cells after 15°C temperature block.
source: In the control cells, PC VII accumulated in the ER in large patches similar to that observed in SLY1 or TANGO1 knockdown cells.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The majority of SEC31 and TANGO1 were localized to specific sites on the ER that contained large patches of PC VII in control cells after temperature block.
source: The majority of SEC31 and TANGO1 were localized to specific sites on the ER that contained large patches of PC VII (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: In SAR1 (A and B) knockdown cells, SEC31 was distributed mostly in the cytoplasm and not associated with the ER exit sites.
source: In SAR1 (A and B) knockdown cells, as expected, SEC31 was distributed mostly in the cytoplasm and not associated with the ER exit sites.
evidence: This is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: TANGO1 was still present at the collagen-enriched patches in SAR1 knockdown cells, suggesting that the TANGO1–Collagen VII binding is independent of TANGO1–SEC23/24 interaction.
source: Interestingly TANGO1 was still present at the collagen-enriched patches, suggesting that the TANGO1–Collagen VII binding is independent of TANGO1–SEC23/24 interaction (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 8B and represents an inference from the observation.

claim: In TANGO1 knockdown cells, the SEC31 positive ER exit sites appeared fewer in number on the collagen patches and more random in localization.
source: In TANGO1 knockdown cells, the SEC31 positive ER exit sites appeared fewer in number on the collagen patches and more random in localization (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: In SLY1-depleted cells, the number and localization of SEC31 sites resembled that of control cells.
source: Interestingly, in SLY1-depleted cells, the number and localization of SEC31 sites resembled that of control cells (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: SLY1 knockdown did not affect the location of TANGO1 at the ER exit sites.
source: SLY1 knockdown did not affect the location of TANGO1 at the ER exit sites.
evidence: This is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Knockdown of SLY1 does not interfere with the capture of PC VII by TANGO1 nor with the assembly of a complete COPII coat.
source: These findings suggest that knockdown of SLY1 does not interfere with the capture of PC VII by TANGO1 nor with the assembly of a complete COPII coat.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the STED microscopy data in Figure 8.

claim: Both knockdown of STX5 and 18 reduced the amount of PC VII being secreted.
source: We observe that both knockdown of STX5 and 18 reduced the amount of PC VII being secreted.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: STX17 had only marginal effect on the secretion of PC VII.
source: STX17 had only marginal effect on the secretion of PC VII (Figure 9B,C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 9B and quantitation in Figure 9C.

claim: Depletion of STX5 reduced the levels of secreted Collagen I in Saos2 cells.
source: We observed a reduction of secreted protein, when cells were treated with siRNAs for STX5.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 9F.

claim: Neither depletion of STX17 nor depletion of STX18 affected the levels of secreted Collagen I.
source: Neither depletion of STX17 nor depletion of STX18 affected the levels of secreted Collagen I (Figure 9F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 9F.

claim: In STX18 and STX5 knockdown samples more than 80% of the cells accumulated PC VII in the ER compared to 25% of the cells in the control.
source: In STX18 and STX5 knockdown samples more than 80% of the cells accumulated PC VII in the ER compared to 25% of the cells in the control (Figure 9D,E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitation of immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 9E.

claim: Accumulation of PC I was only detectable in STX5-depleted cells (80%).
source: Accumulation of PC I was only detectable in STX5-depleted cells (80%).
evidence: This is supported by quantitation of immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 9H.

claim: STX18, like TANGO1 or SLY1 knockdown did not arrest PC I in the ER.
source: STX18, like TANGO1 or SLY1 knockdown did not arrest PC I in the ER (Figure 9G,H).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 9G and quantitation in Figure 9H.

claim: Knockdown of SAR1 A and B inhibits the export of PC VII from the ER.
source: Our new data show that knockdown of SAR1 A and B inhibits the export of PC VII from the ER.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figure 7.

claim: SAR1 dependent recruitment of COPII components is required for general collagen export from the ER.
source: This, combined with the data on the involvement of SEC31 ubiquitination for the export of PC I from the ER (Jin et al., 2012) and Sedlin, a component of the TRAPP II complex that affects the GTPase activity of SAR1 and promotes PC I and II export (Venditti et al., 2012), strongly indicates that SAR1 dependent recruitment of COPII components is required for general collagen export from the ER.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current data and cited literature.

claim: A large number of secretory cargoes bind receptors of the ERGIC53, ERV, and p24 families.
source: A large number of secretory cargoes bind receptors of the ERGIC53, ERV, and p24 families; the receptors in turn bind the inner COPII coat components and are then packed into a standard COPII vesicle (Zanetti et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to Zanetti et al., 2012.

claim: Cargo receptors bind the inner COPII coat components and are then packed into a standard COPII vesicle.
source: A large number of secretory cargoes bind receptors of the ERGIC53, ERV, and p24 families; the receptors in turn bind the inner COPII coat components and are then packed into a standard COPII vesicle (Zanetti et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to Zanetti et al., 2012.

claim: TANGO1 localizes to ER exit sites.
source: Our previous findings indicate that TANGO1, which localizes to ER exit sites, binds PC VII in the lumen and SEC23/24 of the COPII coats on the cytoplasmic site (Saito et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Saito et al., 2009.

claim: The function of TANGO1 is facilitated by cTAGE5.
source: The function of TANGO1 is facilitated by cTAGE5 (Saito et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Saito et al., 2011.

claim: cTAGE5 and TANGO1 interact through their second coiled–coiled domains at the ER exit sites.
source: cTAGE5 and TANGO1 interact through their second (proximal to the proline rich domain) coiled–coiled domains at the ER exit sites.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Saito et al., 2011.

claim: cTAGE5 does not have a luminal domain and cannot bind PC VII directly.
source: cTAGE5 does not have a luminal domain and cannot therefore bind PC VII directly (Saito et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Saito et al., 2011.

claim: The TANGO1–cTAGE5 complex is proposed to stall the COPII vesicles at the ER exit sites as they are being packed with PC VII.
source: The TANGO1–cTAGE5 complex is proposed to stall the COPII vesicles at the ER exit sites as they are being packed with PC VII and this procedure is proposed to result in the production of a transport intermediate for the export of PC VII from the ER (Malhotra and Erlmann, 2011).
evidence: This is a proposed model supported by a citation to Malhotra and Erlmann, 2011.

claim: The process by which PC I in the lumen of the ER is connected to COPII coat components remains unclear.
source: The process by which PC I in the lumen of the ER is connected to COPII coat components remains unclear.
evidence: This is stated as an unknown mechanism.

claim: SLY-1 and the ER-associated t-SNARE STX18 are specifically required for the export of PC VII but not of the general cargoes and PC I.
source: In our experimental conditions, SLY-1 and the ER-associated t-SNARE STX18 are specifically required for the export of PC VII but not of the general cargoes and PC I.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figures 6 and 9.

claim: The sorting of cargoes into different export routes is not driven solely by the size of the secretory cargoes.
source: These findings also highlight that the sorting of cargoes into different export routes is not driven solely by the size of the secretory cargoes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential requirements for PC VII vs PC I export despite similar sizes.

claim: TANGO1 in Drosophila is localized to the basal endoplasmic reticulum specific exit sites.
source: While the mechanism regulating this sorting event remains unclear it is worth highlighting that TANGO1 in Drosophila is localized to the basal endoplasmic reticulum specific exit sites (Lerner et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lerner et al., 2013.

claim: TANGO1 in Drosophila is required for the export of Collagen IV, which is secreted into the basal face of the cells.
source: Moreover, TANGO1 in Drosophila is required for the export of Collagen IV, which is secreted into the basal face of the cells (Lerner et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lerner et al., 2013.

claim: Secretory cargoes may be sorted in the lumen of the ER based on their final destination.
source: It is therefore tempting to propose that secretory cargoes are sorted in the lumen of the ER based on their final destination.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the Drosophila data.

claim: Human cells contain a second SLY1 like protein (SCFD2, Gene ID: 152579).
source: Human cells contain a second SLY1 like protein (SCFD2, Gene ID: 152579).
evidence: This is stated as factual information.

claim: A TANGO1 like protein called MIA2 is expressed only in the liver and small intestine.
source: A TANGO1 like protein called MIA2 that is expressed only in the liver and small intestine has also been identified (Pitman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pitman et al., 2011.

claim: The cargoes exported by SCFD2 and MIA2 are not known.
source: The cargoes exported by these proteins are not known but they could, in combination with SAR1, facilitate the export of other collagens, including Collagen I and perhaps many other bulky molecules, from the ER.
evidence: This is stated as unknown with speculation about potential functions.

claim: SCFD2 and MIA2 could facilitate the export of other collagens, including Collagen I and perhaps many other bulky molecules, from the ER.
source: The cargoes exported by these proteins are not known but they could, in combination with SAR1, facilitate the export of other collagens, including Collagen I and perhaps many other bulky molecules, from the ER.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal.

claim: TANGO1 inhibited the secretion of an artificial cargo ss-HRP in Drosophila S2 cells.
source: At this juncture, it is also important to comment on our original finding that TANGO1 inhibited the secretion of an artificial cargo ss-HRP in Drosophila S2 cells (Bard et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bard et al., 2006.

claim: There is no evidence that TANGO1 binds HRP in the lumen of the ER.
source: There is no evidence that TANGO1 binds HRP in the lumen of the ER and yet both knockdown of TANGO1 and SLY1, as shown here, affect ss-HRP secretion in mammalian cells.
evidence: This is stated as a lack of evidence.

claim: Exogenously expressed ss-HRP or ss-GFP exits the ER by any route available and blocking any one affects its export.
source: We suggest that the exogenously expressed ss-HRP or ss-GFP exits the ER by any route available and blocking any one, for example by TANGO1 or SLY1 knockdown, affects its export because of a block in one of the possible exit routes.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for the ss-HRP data.

claim: It is not known whether SLY1 regulates the activity of the SNARE complex, or helps with the fusion or the disassembly of the SNAREs.
source: The function of SLY1, which is a member of the STXBP/unc-18/SEC1 protein family, remains unclear. For example, it is not known whether SLY1 regulates the activity of the SNARE complex, or helps with the fusion or the disassembly of the SNAREs (Carr and Rizo, 2010).
evidence: This is stated as an unknown mechanism supported by a citation to Carr and Rizo, 2010.

claim: SLY1 at the ER-Golgi interface has been shown to interact with a large number of SNAREs and could thus regulate a number of different SNARE complexes.
source: SLY1 at the ER -Golgi interface has been shown to interact with a large number of SNAREs and could thus regulate a number of different SNARE complexes (Dascher and Balch, 1996; Steegmaier et al., 2000; Yamaguchi et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dascher and Balch, 1996, Steegmaier et al., 2000, and Yamaguchi et al., 2002.

claim: The SNARE complexes reported for the forward trafficking from ER to Golgi are complexes of Golgi t-SNAREs and a specific v-SNARE.
source: So far the SNARE complexes reported for the forward trafficking from ER to Golgi are complexes of Golgi t-SNAREs and a specific v-SNARE.
evidence: This is stated as current knowledge in the field.

claim: There is no evidence that the ER attached t-SNAREs such as STX17, STX18, Sec20 and USE1/P31 are required for the forward transport to the Golgi complex.
source: However, there is no evidence that the ER attached t-SNAREs such as STX17, STX18, Sec20 and USE1/P31 are required for the forward transport to the Golgi complex.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: SLY1 and STX18 function to recycle a specific component from ERGIC/early Golgi cisternae.
source: It could be argued that SLY1 and STX18 function to recycle a specific component, a v-SNARE; for example, from ERGIC/early Golgi cisternae and without which, the cells terminate the export of PC VII out of the ER.
evidence: This is presented as a possible alternative explanation that is then argued against.

claim: Cycling of KDEL containing protein BIP and ERGIC53 as well as the export of other secretory cargoes including the bulky PC I is unaffected by SLY1 or STX18 knockdown.
source: However, cycling of KDEL containing protein BIP and ERGIC53 as well as the export of other secretory cargoes including the bulky PC I is unaffected under these experimental conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figures 5, 6, and 9.

claim: There is no obvious accumulation of PC VII containing large vesicles in between the ER and the Golgi upon SLY1 or TANGO1 knockdown.
source: Additionally, we do not see any obvious accumulation of PC VII containing large vesicles in between the ER and the Golgi.
evidence: This is an observation from the microscopy data.

claim: SLY1 and STX18 are required for the fusion of membranes to the ER to generate an export carrier for PC VII.
source: We therefore favor the possibility that SLY1 and STX18 are required for the fusion of membranes to the ER to generate an export carrier for PC VII.
evidence: This is the authors' favored model based on their data.

claim: A SAR1 dependent reaction initiates the assembly of COPII subunits SEC23/24 at the ER exit sites.
source: A SAR1 dependent reaction initiates the assembly of COPII subunits SEC23/24 at the ER exit sites.
evidence: This is part of the working hypothesis presented in the Discussion.

claim: Recruitment of TANGO1-cTAGE5 complex into the COPII assembly reaction involves its binding of PC VII in the lumen and SEC23/24 on the cytoplasmic site.
source: Recruitment of TANGO1-cTAGE5 complex into this reaction with its binding of PC VII in the lumen and SEC23/24 on the cytoplasmic site.
evidence: This is part of the working hypothesis based on previous findings.

claim: The binding of TANGO1-cTAGE5 to SEC23/24 retards the recruitment of SEC13/31 and prevents premature pinching of membranes.
source: The binding of TANGO1-cTAGE5 to SEC23/24 retards the recruitment of SEC13/31 and prevents premature pinching of membranes (Saito et al., 2009; Malhotra and Erlmann, 2011; Saito et al., 2011).
evidence: This is part of the working hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: ER exit sites containing TANGO1 bound PC VII are concentrated to generate a specific patch (PCP).
source: These ER exit sites containing TANGO1 bound PC VII are then concentrated to generate a specific patch, which for the sake of simplicity we call PCP (PC VII concentrated patch).
evidence: This is part of the working hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: A special pool of recycling membranes (e.g., the ERGIC) fuse with PCP by a reaction that requires SLY1 and STX18.
source: A special pool of recycling membranes; for example, the ERGIC, then fuse with PCP by a reaction that requires SLY1 and STX18.
evidence: This is part of the working hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their data.

claim: As the PCP grows, TANGO1 dissociates from the collagen, which then promotes the recruitment of SEC13/31 to the neck.
source: As the PCP grows, TANGO1 dissociates from the collagen, which then promotes the recruitment of SEC13/31 to the neck.
evidence: This is part of the working hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: TANGO1 dissociation from collagen prevents the packing of TANGO1-cTAGE 5 into the PC VII enriched bud (PEB).
source: This reaction also prevents the packing of TANGO1-cTAGE 5 into the PC VII enriched bud (PEB).
evidence: This is part of the working hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: The neck of the large PEB, concentrated in COPII coats, undergoes fission by the same mechanism as that of a standard COPII vesicle.
source: The neck of this large PEB, concentrated in COPII coats, undergoes fission by the same mechanism as that of a standard COPII vesicle.
evidence: This is part of the working hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: The PC VII enriched large membrane compartment separated from the ER also contains recycled ERGIC membranes.
source: The PC VII enriched large membrane compartment separated from the ER also contains recycled ERGIC membranes.
evidence: This is part of the working hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: The PC VII enriched membrane bound compartment is the first post ER compartment that matures to move PC VII in the anterograde direction for secretion.
source: This membrane bound compartment in principle is the first post ER compartment that matures to move PC VII in the anterograde direction for secretion.
evidence: This is part of the working hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Luini et al. have reported that export of PC I from the ER requires its concentration at a domain close to the ER exit sites, which protrudes and then separates from the ER to generate a PC I enriched carrier.
source: Interestingly, Luini et al. have reported that export of PC I from the ER requires its concentration at a domain close to the ER exit sites, which they suggest protrudes and then separates from the ER to generate a PC I enriched carrier (Mironov et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mironov et al., 2003.

claim: The Luini model is reminiscent of the current scheme in which molecular components such as TANGO1 concentrate PC VII followed by the fusion of membranes to grow the PC VII enriched ER domain.
source: Their model is reminiscent of our scheme in which we place molecular components such as TANGO1 for the concentration of PC VII followed by the fusion of membranes to grow the PC VII enriched ER domain.
evidence: This is a comparison drawn by the authors between their model and previous work.

claim: The TANGO1 mediated concentration of PC VII requires the involvement of COPII components, SEC23/24.
source: However, the TANGO1 mediated concentration of PC VII requires the involvement of COPII components, SEC23/24.
evidence: This is stated as a distinction from the Luini model.

claim: The protrusion visualized by microscopy based analysis might correspond to growth of ER patch by SLY1 and STX18 dependent fusion of the recycling (ERGIC) membranes.
source: Additionally, the protrusion visualized by the microscopy based analysis might correspond to growth of ER patch by SLY1 and STX18 dependent fusion of the recycling (ERGIC) membranes.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation of the Luini data in light of the current findings.
